Appendix A Clairvoyant Scheduling Guarantees

The clairvoyant benchmark has three useful forms. Area-order greedy is nearly optimal when every job is small compared with the memory budget. For general instances, splitting jobs by full rectangle width and combining the two resulting schedules gives a constant approximation. A direct rectangle packing argument gives a smaller constant by using a known strip packing guarantee as a black box. The schedules below reserve the full rectangle width of each active job:

ℓi≜si+oi,\ell_{i}\triangleq s_{i}+o_{i},

i.e., reserving the full rectangle of each job.

A.1 Large-Memory Case

The large-memory case is a KV-cache analogue of the small-demand WSVF guarantee for capacitated machines [Cohen et al., 2024, Theorem 1].

Theorem 4 (Bounded-width area-order greedy).

Fix ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). Suppose that every job in 𝒥\mathcal{J} satisfies

ℓi≤ε​M.\ell_{i}\leq\varepsilon M.

Then the schedule produced by Greedy satisfies

Greedy​(𝒥)≤(1+21−ε)​Opt​(𝒥).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J})\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{1-\varepsilon}\right)\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}).
Proof.

Let Sπ⁡(r)S_{\pi(r)} be the start time of job π⁡(r)\pi(r). Before time Sπ⁡(r)S_{\pi(r)}, if job π⁡(r)\pi(r) has not yet been admitted, then the next unstarted job has reserved width at most ε​M\varepsilon M. Thus, after the greedy admission step in each such round, the active reserved width is larger than (1−ε)​M(1-\varepsilon)M. All active jobs before time Sπ⁡(r)S_{\pi(r)} belong to {π⁡(1),…,π⁡(r−1)}\{\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(r-1)\}. Therefore,

Sπ⁡(r)≤1(1−ε)​M​∑q=1r−1ℓπ⁡(q)​oπ⁡(q).S_{\pi(r)}\leq\frac{1}{(1-\varepsilon)M}\sum_{q=1}^{r-1}\ell_{\pi(q)}o_{\pi(q)}.

Since job π⁡(r)\pi(r) completes oπ⁡(r)o_{\pi(r)} rounds after it starts,

Cπ⁡(r)≤oπ⁡(r)+1(1−ε)​M​∑q=1r−1ℓπ⁡(q)​oπ⁡(q).C_{\pi(r)}\leq o_{\pi(r)}+\frac{1}{(1-\varepsilon)M}\sum_{q=1}^{r-1}\ell_{\pi(q)}o_{\pi(q)}.

Summing over all ranks gives

Greedy​(𝒥)≤∑i∈𝒥oi+1(1−ε)​M​∑q=1n(n−q)​ℓπ⁡(q)​oπ⁡(q).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J})\leq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}}o_{i}+\frac{1}{(1-\varepsilon)M}\sum_{q=1}^{n}(n-q)\ell_{\pi(q)}o_{\pi(q)}.

For every job ii,

ℓi​oi=si​oi+oi2≤2​Ai.\ell_{i}o_{i}=s_{i}o_{i}+o_{i}^{2}\leq 2A_{i}.

Hence

Greedy​(𝒥)≤∑i∈𝒥oi+2(1−ε)​M​∑q=1n(n−q)​Aπ⁡(q).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J})\leq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}}o_{i}+\frac{2}{(1-\varepsilon)M}\sum_{q=1}^{n}(n-q)A_{\pi(q)}.

Since π\pi is the nondecreasing area order, Lemmas 3 and 1 give

Greedy​(𝒥)≤(1+21−ε)​Opt​(𝒥).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J})\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{1-\varepsilon}\right)\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}).

∎

Corollary 2 (Large-memory area-order greedy).

If maxi∈𝒥⁡ℓi=o⁡(M),\max_{i\in\mathcal{J}}{\ell_{i}}=o(M), then the clairvoyant area-order schedule in Theorem 4 is a (3+o⁡(1))(3+o(1))-approximation. Equivalently,

Greedy​(𝒥)≤(3+o⁡(1))​Opt​(𝒥).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J})\leq(3+o(1))\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}).

A.2 General Case via Black-Box Meta-Scheduling

For a general clairvoyant instance, view each job as a rectangle with width ℓi\ell_{i} and height oio_{i}. The jobs are separated by rectangle width. The small-width part uses Greedy with the true full widths. The large-width part uses the same Greedy routine on an auxiliary instance in which every job reserves rectangle width MM. The two schedules are merged by the black-box meta-scheduler of Section 6.1.

Lemma 12 (Full-width auxiliary greedy call).

For λ=1/2\lambda=1/2, the auxiliary instance 𝒥>λM\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}^{M} defined in Algorithm 6 satisfies

Greedy​(𝒥>λM)≤4​Opt​(𝒥>λ).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}^{M})\leq 4\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}).
Proof.

Set m≜|𝒥>λ|m\triangleq{\left|\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}\right|}. Let π⁡(1),…,π⁡(m)\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(m) be the nondecreasing true area order of 𝒥>λ\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}. In the auxiliary instance, every job reserves MM and has area key M​oiMo_{i}. Thus Greedy runs one job at a time in nondecreasing oio_{i}. This order has no larger total completion time than the sequential schedule that follows the order π\pi, so

Greedy​(𝒥>λM)≤∑r=1m(m−r+1)​oπ⁡(r).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}^{M})\leq\sum_{r=1}^{m}(m-r+1)o_{\pi(r)}.

For every i∈𝒥>λi\in\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda},

Ai≥ℓi​oi2>M​oi4.A_{i}\geq\frac{\ell_{i}o_{i}}{2}>\frac{Mo_{i}}{4}.

It follows that

Greedy​(𝒥>λM)≤4M​∑r=1m(m−r+1)​Aπ⁡(r)≤4​Opt​(𝒥>λ),\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}^{M})\leq\frac{4}{M}\sum_{r=1}^{m}(m-r+1)A_{\pi(r)}\leq 4\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}),

where the last inequality follows from Lemma 1 applied to 𝒥>λ\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}. ∎

Theorem 5.

The schedule produced by Clairvoyant-Mix satisfies

Clairvoyant-Mix​(𝒥)≤28​Opt​(𝒥).\textup{{Clairvoyant-Mix}}(\mathcal{J})\leq 28\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}).
Proof.

For λ=1/2\lambda=1/2, the same proof as Theorem 4 gives

Greedy​(𝒥≤λ)≤5​Opt​(𝒥≤λ),\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{\leq\lambda})\leq 5\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}_{\leq\lambda}),

and Lemma 12 gives

Greedy​(𝒥>λM)≤4​Opt​(𝒥>λ).\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}^{M})\leq 4\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}).

The branch-dependent bound in Lemma 10 gives a factor of 55 for the first branch and a factor of 77 for the second branch. Since Algorithm 6 places the small-width branch first, it gives

Clairvoyant-Mix​(𝒥)≤5​Greedy​(𝒥≤λ)+7​Greedy​(𝒥>λM).\textup{{Clairvoyant-Mix}}(\mathcal{J})\leq 5\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{\leq\lambda})+7\textup{{Greedy}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}^{M}).

Together with Lemma 2, this implies

Clairvoyant-Mix​(𝒥)≤25​Opt​(𝒥≤λ)+28​Opt​(𝒥>λ)≤28​Opt​(𝒥).\textup{{Clairvoyant-Mix}}(\mathcal{J})\leq 25\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}_{\leq\lambda})+28\,\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda})\leq 28\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}).

This proves the theorem. ∎

A.3 General Case with Direct Rectangle-Packing

This subsection gives a second clairvoyant bound using a stronger geometric primitive. The previous two subsections use area-order scheduling directly; here we call a strip packing algorithm as a black box, which gives a stronger makespan guarantee for each stage. The conversion from stage makespan guarantees to total completion time follows the doubling framework of the single-machine capacitated scheduling algorithm of [Cohen et al., 2024, Theorem 7.1]. Two simplifications apply in the present unweighted rectangle instance:

  • •

    The knapsack selection step for weighted rectangles becomes the exact prefix after sorting by rectangle area.

  • •

    For rectangles with width at most MM, height at most LL, and total area at most M​LML, the 22-approximation algorithm by Steinberg [1997] packs them in height at most 2​L2L.

These two changes give an 88-approximation for the rectangle instance, improving the 12+ε12+\varepsilon factor from the corresponding framework of Cohen et al. [2024]. The conversion from KV-cache jobs to rectangles loses another factor of 22 against the area lower bound, yielding the 1616-approximation below.

Theorem 6.

The schedule produced by PackAndSchedule satisfies

PackAndSchedule​(𝒥)≤16​Opt​(𝒥).\textup{{PackAndSchedule}}(\mathcal{J})\leq 16\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}).
Proof.

After stage rr, the algorithm has completed at least |𝒞r|{\left|\mathcal{C}_{r}\right|} jobs by time

2​∑q=0r2q<4⋅2r.2\sum_{q=0}^{r}2^{q}<4\cdot 2^{r}.

The optimal schedule completes at most |𝒞r|{\left|\mathcal{C}_{r}\right|} jobs by time 2r−12^{r-1}. To see that, let 𝒞r⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star}_{r} be the jobs completed by an optimal schedule by that time. Every job in 𝒞r⋆\mathcal{C}^{\star}_{r} has oi≤2ro_{i}\leq 2^{r}, and these jobs have total rectangle area at most

∑i∈𝒞r⋆ℓi​oi≤2​∑i∈𝒞r⋆Ai≤M​2r.\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}^{\star}_{r}}\ell_{i}o_{i}\leq 2\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}^{\star}_{r}}A_{i}\leq M2^{r}.

By the maximality of the prefix 𝒞r\mathcal{C}_{r}, this implies |𝒞r⋆|≤|𝒞r|{\left|\mathcal{C}^{\star}_{r}\right|}\leq{\left|\mathcal{C}_{r}\right|}.

For ranks |𝒞r−1|+1,…,|𝒞r|{\left|\mathcal{C}_{r-1}\right|}+1,\ldots,{\left|\mathcal{C}_{r}\right|} with r≥0r\geq 0 (using the convention 𝒞−1=∅\mathcal{C}_{-1}=\varnothing), the algorithm completes these ranks by time less than 4⋅2r4\cdot 2^{r}, while the optimal schedule cannot complete these ranks before time 2r−22^{r-2}. Summing over all ranks gives PackAndSchedule​(𝒥)≤16​Opt\textup{{PackAndSchedule}}(\mathcal{J})\leq 16\textup{{Opt}}. ∎

Remark 4.

The same argument improves the single-machine weighted capacitated scheduling bound of [Cohen et al., 2024, Theorem 7.1] from 12+ε12+\varepsilon to 8+ε8+\varepsilon. It keeps their resource-augmented knapsack step, adds the natural scale eligibility condition on processing times (ℰr\mathcal{E}_{r} in Algorithm 7), and replaces the factor-33 packing step based on Jansen and Zhang [2007] by Steinberg’s factor-22 strip packing theorem.

Appendix B Complete Non-Clairvoyant Rectangle Strip Scheduling

The rectangle strip guarantee in Theorem 2 assumes a useful width range. This section removes that assumption by mixing two rectangle strip schedulers through the black-box meta-scheduler.

Theorem 7.

For every rectangle strip instance with wi≤Mw_{i}\leq M for all i∈𝒥i\in\mathcal{J}, there is a non-clairvoyant scheduling algorithm whose total completion time is within a constant factor of the optimal clairvoyant total completion time:

RectMix​(𝒥)=O⁡(1)⋅Optrect​(𝒥).\textup{{RectMix}}(\mathcal{J})=O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{rect}}(\mathcal{J}).
Proof.

Run Algorithm 8 with λ=(149−11)/2\lambda=(\sqrt{149}-11)/2. By Theorem 2, the two branch ratios are

4+81−λand4+8λ.4+\frac{8}{1-\lambda}\qquad\text{and}\qquad 4+\frac{8}{\lambda}.

By Lemma 10, the first branch loses a factor of 55 and the second branch loses a factor of 77. Hence

RectMix​(𝒥)≤5​(4+81−λ)​Optrect​(𝒥≤λ)+7​(4+8λ)​Optrect​(𝒥>λ).\textup{{RectMix}}(\mathcal{J})\leq 5\left(4+\frac{8}{1-\lambda}\right)\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{rect}}(\mathcal{J}_{\leq\lambda})+7\left(4+\frac{8}{\lambda}\right)\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{rect}}(\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda}).

The chosen λ\lambda makes both coefficients equal to 72+4​14972+4\sqrt{149}. Since 𝒥≤λ\mathcal{J}_{\leq\lambda} and 𝒥>λ\mathcal{J}_{>\lambda} partition 𝒥\mathcal{J}, Lemma 2 gives the theorem. ∎

Lemma 15 (Response subset control).

Fix a response-heavy set ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*} and a deterministic order used by Response. For each i∈ℛ∗i\in\mathcal{R}^{*}, let CiRC^{\textup{{R}}}_{i} be the completion time of ii in Response​(ℛ∗)\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{R}^{*}). Then, for every 𝒥′⊆ℛ∗\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{R}^{*} and every i∈𝒥′i\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}, job ii completes in Response​(𝒥′)\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}) by time CiRC^{\textup{{R}}}_{i}.

Proof.

Fix any job i∈𝒥′i\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}, and let rr be the first phase with τr≥oi\tau_{r}\geq o_{i}. Run Response​(𝒥′)\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}) using the order induced by the fixed order on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. By Lemma 9, job ii completes in phase rr in both Response​(𝒥′)\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}) and Response​(ℛ∗)\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{R}^{*}). For every phase q<rq<r, whether a job is considered in that phase depends only on its prompt length, response length, and the cap sequence. Thus the jobs considered in the run on 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime} form a subsequence of the jobs considered in the run on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. For every remaining job in this subsequence, its rank is no larger than its rank in the run on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. Since the SPS start offset is ⌊j​τq/kq⌋\lfloor j\tau_{q}/k_{q}\rfloor for rank jj, each remaining job starts no later in the run on 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime} than in the run on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. The real running time of every remaining job in phase qq is unchanged, so the duration of phase qq in the run on 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime} is no larger than the duration of phase qq in the run on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. The same subsequence property holds inside phase rr: the rank of job ii in the run on 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime} is at most its rank in the run on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}, so the SPS start offset of job ii is no later in the run on 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime} than in the run on ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. After job ii starts in phase rr, the remaining time until completion is oio_{i} in both runs. Combining these components gives the claim. ∎

Appendix D Alternative Objectives

This appendix gives two extensions of the meta-scheduling framework.

  • •

    Section D.1 shows that the same algorithm is also constant-competitive for makespan.

  • •

    Section D.2 extends the routing framework to total completion time with online arrivals.

For online arrivals, the natural latency objective is total flow time. Under (oblivious) adversarial arrivals, however, online KV-cache scheduling admits an Ω⁡(n)\Omega(\sqrt{n}) lower bound on the competitive ratio for total flow time, even in the identical-prompt special case [Jaillet et al., 2025, Feng et al., 2026]. Total completion time is the closest feasible alternative: for a fixed arrival instance, the two objectives induce the same optimal schedules. Online completion-time objectives have also been studied in classical scheduling [Epstein and van Stee, 2003, van Stee and Poutré, 2005].

D.1 Makespan

For a job set 𝒥′⊆𝒥\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{J}, let Optspan​(𝒥′)\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime}) be the optimal clairvoyant makespan for scheduling exactly the jobs in 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime}. For a schedule produced by an algorithm Alg, let Makespan​[Alg​(𝒥′)]{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Alg}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime})\right] denote its makespan.

Lemma 16 (Makespan lower bounds).

For every 𝒥′⊆𝒥\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{J},

Optspan​(𝒥′)≥maxi∈𝒥′⁡oi,Optspan​(𝒥′)≥1M​∑i∈𝒥′Ai.\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime})\geq\max_{i\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}o_{i},\qquad\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime})\geq\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}A_{i}.

The first bound is the processing requirement of the longest job. The second follows because all memory-time areas of jobs must be supplied. We use the branch sets and capped small instance from Section 6.2.

Proposition 4 (Branch makespan bounds).

Set Λ=M/4\Lambda=M/4 and α=2\alpha=2. Then

Makespan​[Rect​(ℒ)],Makespan​[Rect​(𝒮^)],Makespan​[Response​(ℛ∗)]{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Rect}}(\mathcal{L})\right],\quad{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Rect}}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}})\right],\quad{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{R}^{*})\right]

are all O​(1)⋅Optspan​(𝒥)O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}).

Proof.

For either rectangle branch instance 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime}, Lemma 5 implies, after taking the maximum over jobs in 𝒥′\mathcal{J}^{\prime},

Makespan​[Rect​(𝒥′)]=O⁡(maxi∈𝒥′⁡pi+1M​∑i∈𝒥′AiRect),{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Rect}}(\mathcal{J}^{\prime})\right]=O\left(\max_{i\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}p_{i}+\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}^{\prime}}A_{i}^{\textup{{Rect}}}\right),

using the same width-range conditions as in the proofs of Propositions 2 and 3. For the large branch, AiRect≤4​AiA_{i}^{\textup{{Rect}}}\leq 4A_{i}. For the prompt-heavy branch, the capped rectangle area is at most 2​Ai2A_{i}. Thus both rectangle branch makespans are O​(1)⋅Optspan​(𝒥)O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}) by Lemma 16.

For the response-heavy branch, the phase-duration estimate used in the proof of Theorem 3, summed over geometric response caps, gives

Makespan​[Response​(ℛ∗)]=O⁡(maxi∈ℛ∗⁡oi+1M​∑i∈ℛ∗oi2).{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Response}}(\mathcal{R}^{*})\right]=O\left(\max_{i\in\mathcal{R}^{*}}o_{i}+\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{R}^{*}}o_{i}^{2}\right).

Here the geometric caps bound the linear contribution by the largest response length, and the phase-efficiency term contributes the quadratic area term. Since every job in ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*} is response-heavy, oi2≤2​Aio_{i}^{2}\leq 2A_{i}. Another application of Lemma 16 completes the proof. ∎

The following theorem gives the makespan extension.

Theorem 8.

For every feasible batch KV-cache scheduling instance with arbitrary prompt lengths and arbitrary response lengths, there is a fully non-clairvoyant scheduling algorithm whose makespan is within a constant factor of the optimal clairvoyant makespan:

Makespan​[Alg​(𝒥)]=O⁡(1)⋅Optspan​(𝒥).{\textup{{Makespan}}}\!\left[\textup{{Alg}}(\mathcal{J})\right]=O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}).
Proof.

Set Λ=M/4\Lambda=M/4 and α=2\alpha=2, and run the routing meta-scheduler Route in Algorithm 4. Let

T=max⁡{maxi∈ℒ⁡CiL,maxi∈𝒮⁡CiP,maxi∈ℛ∗⁡CiR}.T=\max\left\{\max_{i\in\mathcal{L}}C^{\textup{{L}}}_{i},\;\max_{i\in\mathcal{S}}C^{\textup{{P}}}_{i},\;\max_{i\in\mathcal{R}^{*}}C^{\textup{{R}}}_{i}\right\}.

By the subset-control discussion in Section 6.2, every current branch call completes or certifies its remaining jobs within the corresponding reference bound. Choose the first stage rr with 2r≥T2^{r}\geq T. In this stage, the prompt-heavy branch call completes all remaining jobs in 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*} and certifies all remaining jobs in ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}. The certified jobs then move to ℛ\mathcal{R}, and the following response-heavy branch call completes them; the large branch call completes all large jobs. Thus all jobs finish by the end of the stage. The total time through that stage is O⁡(2r)=O⁡(T)O(2^{r})=O(T). The same bounds used in Proposition 4 give T=O⁡(1)⋅Optspan​(𝒥)T=O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{span}}(\mathcal{J}), which proves the theorem. ∎

D.2 Total Completion Time with Online Arrivals

Each job ii now has an arrival time ai∈ℕa_{i}\in\mathbb{N}. Before time aia_{i}, job ii is not visible to the scheduler. At time aia_{i}, its prompt length sis_{i} becomes known, while its response length oio_{i} is still unknown until completion. Let Optarr​(𝒥)\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{arr}}(\mathcal{J}) be the optimal total completion time of a clairvoyant schedule that knows all jobs and response lengths in advance, but may process job ii only after time aia_{i}.

Lemma 17 (Online-arrival lower bounds).
Optarr​(𝒥)≥Opt​(𝒥),Optarr​(𝒥)≥∑i∈𝒥(ai+oi).\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{arr}}(\mathcal{J})\geq\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}),\qquad\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{arr}}(\mathcal{J})\geq\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}}\left(a_{i}+o_{i}\right).

The first bound follows by removing arrival constraints. The second follows because job ii cannot complete before time ai+oia_{i}+o_{i}.

The online scheduler uses the same pool convention: newly arrived jobs enter either ℒ\mathcal{L} or 𝒫\mathcal{P}, certified but unfinished jobs move to ℛ\mathcal{R}, and completed jobs are removed from their branch pools.

The following theorem gives the online-arrival extension.

Theorem 9.

For every feasible online-arrival KV-cache scheduling instance with arbitrary prompt lengths, arbitrary response lengths, and arbitrary arrival times, there is an online non-clairvoyant scheduling algorithm whose total completion time is within a constant factor of the optimal clairvoyant total completion time among schedules that process each job only after its arrival:

RouteOnline​(𝒥)=O⁡(1)⋅Optarr​(𝒥).\textup{{RouteOnline}}(\mathcal{J})=O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{arr}}(\mathcal{J}).
Proof.

Set Λ=M/4\Lambda=M/4 and α=2\alpha=2, and run the online-arrival routing meta-scheduler in Algorithm 9. The online arrival constraint only delays the time at which a job can enter the routing process. A job arriving at time aia_{i} is admitted at the start of the first stage that begins at or after aia_{i}; by the doubling schedule, the elapsed time before that stage is O⁡(ai)O(a_{i}). After this prefix, the same routing calculation as in the batch proof applies to job ii, using the reference bounds CiL,CiP,CiRC^{\textup{{L}}}_{i},C^{\textup{{P}}}_{i},C^{\textup{{R}}}_{i} as in the proof of Theorem 1. The current branch calls are on subsets of the corresponding reference instances, so the same subset arguments apply. Thus

CiRouteOnline\displaystyle C_{i}^{\textup{{RouteOnline}}} =O⁡(ai+CiL)\displaystyle=O(a_{i}+C^{\textup{{L}}}_{i}) for every ​i∈ℒ,\displaystyle\text{for every }i\in\mathcal{L},
CiRouteOnline\displaystyle C_{i}^{\textup{{RouteOnline}}} =O⁡(ai+CiP)\displaystyle=O(a_{i}+C^{\textup{{P}}}_{i}) for every ​i∈𝒫∗,\displaystyle\text{for every }i\in\mathcal{P}^{*},
CiRouteOnline\displaystyle C_{i}^{\textup{{RouteOnline}}} =O⁡(ai+CiP+CiR)\displaystyle=O(a_{i}+C^{\textup{{P}}}_{i}+C^{\textup{{R}}}_{i}) for every ​i∈ℛ∗.\displaystyle\text{for every }i\in\mathcal{R}^{*}.

Summing over all jobs gives the same three branch sums as in the proof of Theorem 1, plus the arrival term ∑i∈𝒥ai\sum_{i\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i}. The branch sums are bounded by O​(1)⋅Opt​(𝒥)O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J}), while the arrival term is bounded by Lemma 17 and Opt​(𝒥)≤Optarr​(𝒥)\textup{{Opt}}(\mathcal{J})\leq\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{arr}}(\mathcal{J}). Therefore RouteOnline​(𝒥)=O⁡(1)⋅Optarr​(𝒥)\textup{{RouteOnline}}(\mathcal{J})=O(1)\cdot\textup{{Opt}}_{\mathrm{arr}}(\mathcal{J}). ∎
